title: Dividend Decision
outcomes: Explain forms and determinants of dividend policy.
Apply Walter, Gordon and traditional models.
Explain stable dividend policies and Lintner's model.

meta.exam_tip: Compare r with Ke before any calculation — it tells you the answer to "optimal payout".

concepts.title: Dividend decision, forms of dividend and determinants
body: The dividend decision splits earnings between distribution and retention; it affects shareholder wealth, financing needs and signalling.
Forms: cash dividend; stock dividend (bonus shares — no cash outflow, more shares); share buy-back as an alternative way of returning cash; interim and final dividends.

Determinants: legal restrictions (dividend out of profits, Companies Act rules), liquidity, growth needs and access to capital, stability of earnings, shareholders' preference and tax, inflation, and covenants in loan agreements.
concepts.analogy: Dividend policy is a trade-off between cash in shareholders' hands today and growth tomorrow.
concepts.work: A start-up with high-return projects usually retains all earnings.

concepts.title: Relevance theories: Walter, Gordon, traditional
body: Walter: P = [D + (r/Ke)(E − D)] ÷ Ke. If r > Ke (growth firm), retention raises price — optimal payout 0%; if r < Ke (declining firm), full payout is optimal; if r = Ke (normal firm), payout does not matter. Assumes all financing from retention, constant r and Ke, infinite life.
Gordon: P = E(1 − b) ÷ (Ke − br), where b is retention ratio and br is growth. Conclusions mirror Walter's; with uncertainty, investors value near dividends more ("bird in hand").
Traditional (Graham and Dodd): P = m(D + E/3), giving dividends more weight than retained earnings.
concepts.analogy: Relevance theories link the best payout to whether the firm earns more than shareholders require.
concepts.work: Under Gordon, EPS ₹20, b = 0.6, r = 15%, Ke = 12% gives g = 9% and P = ₹8 ÷ 3% = ₹266.67.

concepts.title: Irrelevance: Modigliani–Miller
body: Modigliani and Miller argue that, in perfect markets with no taxes, no transaction or flotation costs and fixed investment policy, dividend policy does not affect firm value; value depends on earnings power and investment decisions.
P0 = (D1 + P1) ÷ (1 + Ke); shares issued to finance investment: Δn = [I − (E − nD1)] ÷ P1. Paying a dividend lowers P1 by exactly the dividend, and the new issue offsets the cash paid.
Criticisms: taxes on dividends and gains differ, flotation costs exist, investors face transaction costs, information asymmetry gives dividends a signalling role, and markets are not perfect.
concepts.analogy: MM: what you get as dividend you lose in share price, when markets are perfect.
concepts.work: A ₹5 dividend on a share that would be worth ₹110 leaves the share at ₹105 — the holder's wealth is unchanged.

concepts.title: Dividend policy in practice: stability and Lintner
body: Stable dividend policies (constant dividend per share, constant payout ratio, or a small regular dividend plus extra) are popular because investors value predictability and signals.
Lintner's model: firms have a target payout ratio and adjust dividends gradually towards it: D1 = D0 + [(EPS × target payout) − D0] × adjustment factor.
Stock dividends and splits do not change wealth directly but improve marketability and may signal confidence.
concepts.analogy: Managers smooth dividends because cutting them sends a bad signal.
concepts.work: Target payout 50%, EPS rises from ₹8 to ₹12, previous dividend ₹4, adjustment 0.5: new dividend ₹5.

illustrations.title: Should a growth firm pay out?
illustrations.q: EPS ₹10; cost of equity 10%. Using Walter's model, find the share price at 40% and 100% payout when (a) return on investment r = 15% and (b) r = 8%. What is the optimal payout in each case?

solution.text: When r = Ke the price is the same at any payout — dividend policy does not matter.

illustrations.title: Testing MM
illustrations.q: A firm has 1,00,000 shares at ₹100 each; cost of equity 10%. It expects net income of ₹10 lakh, plans investment of ₹20 lakh and is considering a dividend of ₹5 per share. Under MM, find the year-end price if the dividend is paid, the number of new shares needed, and show the firm's value is unchanged.

solution.text: Without a dividend the year-end price would be ₹110, fewer shares would be issued, and the value is still ₹1,00,00,000 — so dividend policy is irrelevant under MM's assumptions.

jobs.title: Board note on dividend
jobs.situation: The CFO asks whether to raise the dividend or fund a new plant from profits.
steps: Compare expected project return with the cost of equity.
Assess cash and access to external funds.
jobs.takeaway: If retained profits earn more than shareholders' required return, retention usually adds value.

mcqs.q: Under Walter's model, a growth firm (r > Ke) should:
mcqs.explain: Each rupee retained earns more than shareholders require, raising price. In practice: high-growth tech firms pay little dividend.
With full payout P = 8 ÷ 0.10 = ₹80. In practice: r does not matter at 100% payout.

mcqs.q: In Gordon's model, growth g equals:
mcqs.explain: Growth comes from retained earnings reinvested at r. In practice: requires Ke > g.

mcqs.q: Gordon: E = ₹10, b = 0.4, r = 10%, Ke = 12%. Price:
mcqs.explain: D = 6; g = 4%; P = 6 ÷ (0.12 − 0.04) = ₹75. In practice: sensitive to Ke − g.

options: Perfect capital markets with no taxes
Different tax on dividends and gains
mcqs.explain: MM rely on perfect markets, no taxes and fixed investment policy. In practice: real markets violate these.

mcqs.q: Under MM, P0 ₹50, Ke 10%, D1 ₹2. P1:
mcqs.explain: P1 = 50 × 1.10 − 2 = ₹53. In practice: without dividend P1 = ₹55.

mcqs.q: The traditional model of Graham and Dodd is:
mcqs.explain: It weights dividends three times as heavily as retained earnings. In practice: reflects investor preference for dividends.

options: Adjust dividends gradually towards a target payout
Change dividends every year with earnings
mcqs.explain: Dividends are smoothed using an adjustment factor. In practice: explains sticky dividends.

summary: r > Ke retain; r < Ke distribute; r = Ke irrelevant.
Lintner: gradual adjustment to target payout.
traps: Bonus shares do not change shareholder wealth by themselves.

viva.q: What does Walter say about a normal firm?
viva.model: When the return on investment equals the cost of equity, the share price is the same at every payout, so dividend policy is irrelevant.
Price equals earnings times one minus retention ratio, divided by cost of equity minus retention ratio times return.
In perfect markets the value of a firm depends on its earning power and investment policy; the dividend paid is offset by a fall in share price, so payout does not matter.
Taxes treat dividends and capital gains differently, and flotation and transaction costs exist.

viva.q: Why do companies keep dividends stable?
viva.model: Because investors value predictable income and a cut sends a negative signal about future earnings.

cases.title: Aarohi Tech Ltd.
cases.case: Aarohi Tech Ltd.: EPS ₹20; cost of equity 12%; return on investment 18%. The board debates a 30% or 70% payout. Use Walter's model.

mcqs.explain: D = 6; P = [6 + (0.18 ÷ 0.12) × 14] ÷ 0.12 = 27 ÷ 0.12 = ₹225. In practice: retention adds value here.
D = 14; P = [14 + 1.5 × 6] ÷ 0.12 = 23 ÷ 0.12 = ₹191.67. In practice: higher payout lowers price for a growth firm.
Since r (18%) exceeds Ke (12%), retaining everything maximises price (₹250). In practice: consider shareholder cash needs.

mcqs.q: Under MM, the choice of payout would:
mcqs.explain: MM hold dividend policy irrelevant in perfect markets. In practice: taxes and signalling make it relevant.
